log.why: E11 splits Ticket 1's prior nearly in half (0.465 vs 0.535), maximizing expected information gain.
Treating at 3 uM splits Ticket 2's prior probability almost evenly (0.488 vs 0.512) for maximum information gain.
Testing top candidate sodA (0.357) directly can yield a publishable posterior if lost, or narrow down to hisG and metJ.
E2 (1 µM) bisects Ticket 2's posterior (0.558 vs 0.443) while we wait for Ticket 1's E5 result.
HisG has 0.500 posterior and time is shorter on Ticket 1, so knocking out hisG maximally splits the remaining probability mass.
Retesting 3 uM checks the larger upper tail (0.207) and can boost 3 uM confidence from 0.670 to over 0.90 before publishing.
E4 splits the posterior mass nearly in half (0.555 vs 0.445) and incubates while we publish Ticket 1.
hisG has a very strong 0.918 posterior with only 23s remaining, making immediate publication optimal.
E4 splits Ticket 3's probability mass nearly evenly at 10 uM while leaving time to publish Ticket 2 during incubation.
With only 10s left, no plate can finish in time, and publishing at 0.424 posterior beats letting the ticket expire.
Ticket 3 has 19s left; testing 30 µM splits the remaining posterior mass between 30 µM and higher doses before publishing.
With 11 s left and E5 needing 6 s before a ~5 s write-up, waiting risks expiration; 30 µM (0.470) has positive expected value now.
Testing top candidate gyrA (0.413 prior) starts incubation now while leaving time to publish expiring Ticket 4 next.
With 8s left on Ticket 4, no experiment can finish, and publishing ompF (0.291) beats expiration penalty in expected value.
With only 14 s left in the round, gyrA has a strong 0.888 posterior and there is no time to incubate and publish another plate.
With 9 s left, no experiment can finish, and publishing at 0.198 posterior has negative expected value.
